Good instinct — a strong thumbnail is what makes a portfolio tile actually get clicked. Here's how to approach it with Nano Banana Pro.

First, a key decision: a thumbnail isn't just a frame from the video. It's a composed key art image — usually one strong hero subject, breathing room for a title or logo, and a clear focal point that reads even at small sizes. So you're not just upscaling a still; you're directing NBP to build a poster.

The workflow

Pick your strongest hero frame from the video as the input image — ideally one with a clean silhouette of the runner and some negative space. NBP works best when it has a real anchor to composite against rather than generating from scratch, and it keeps your locked character consistent. If your best motion moment doesn't have room for text, that's fine — you'll tell NBP to extend the frame.

Then prompt it conversationally, the way NBP likes. Something like:

Take this runner and place them in a wide cinematic key-art composition. Keep the character exactly as-is. Extend the environment with clean negative space on the upper left for a title. Dramatic low-angle lighting, deep shadows, a single warm rim light catching the edge of the body. Cinematic color grade, slightly desaturated with crushed blacks. Premium athletic-brand poster energy. 16:9.

A few principles that matter here, consistent with how you already run NBP:

The lighting adapts to the poster mood, not the original frame — push it more dramatic and contrasty than a mid-shot would naturally be, since key art is allowed to be louder than the film itself. Keep the character locked; only the environment and light should change. And resist the urge to add elements — one runner, one light source, one mood. Thumbnails fail when they're busy.

For aspect ratio: your portfolio card looks roughly 16:9, so generate at 16:9 and leave the title space deliberately empty. Don't have NBP render the text — typography always looks cleaner laid on afterward in Premiere, Figma, or even Canva.

One thing to decide before you prompt: do you want the thumbnail to match the warm tobacco grade of your firstshot.png anchor, or go cooler and sharper like Man_Running_Towards.png? For an Adidas piece I'd lean toward the sharper, higher-contrast direction — it reads more "performance brand" — but the warm grade would feel more premium-cinematic. Either works; just commit to one so the prompt is clean.
